newsitem.title: BELGIUM: LABOUR COSTS - STILL BELGIUM'S ACHILLES HEEL?.
newsitem.headline: LABOUR COSTS - STILL BELGIUM'S ACHILLES HEEL?.

text.p: The decision by French car maker Renault SA to close its Belgian plant in its fight for greater competitiveness has raised questions about the level of labour costs in the country.

Partly due to past fiscal generosity which had to be undone with tax rises to cap rising government debt and make Belgium fit for Europe's single currency union, the bulk of the total package of income taxes and social security contributions in Belgium makes having staff a costly affair for employers.
But are labour costs worse in Belgium than elsewhere?

For Renault the decision to close its Renault Industrie Belgique> assembly plant in Vilvoorde near Brussels with a workforce of 3,100 is about dealing with overcapacity in the company and the industry, but also about cost-cutting.

Commenting on the closure Belgian employers, further angering unions already upset about the job losses, have pointed the finger at high labour costs, echoing comments by central bank president Alfons Verplaetse.

Reducing labour cost would boost the job-creating effect of economic growth and Belgian unions should focus on job creation rather than wage rises, the central banker said recently, urging Belgians to follow the example of their Dutch neighbours.

"It is of material importance Belgium gets a grip on wage costs," employers umbrella organisation FEB said, noting that if between 1987 and 1993 wage cost trends here had matched those in neighbouring countries, 69,000 jobs would have been created.
"Our Dutch neighbours are showing us the way," FEB said.
At the end of 1996 9.4 percent of Belgium's labour force was unemployed compared to just 6.4 percent in the Netherlands.

A recent study by German car association VDA showed Spanish and British car workers cost respectively 28 and 27 marks per hour compared with 44.6 marks in Belgium and 62.4 marks in Germany -- where automobile labour costs are the highest.
Spain is one of the countries to which Renault is relocating output from Vilvoorde. It is typically one of the EU regions where labour costs are lower and investment incentives higher.
Belgian unions are passing the buck. They say they have been modest in their demands, noting one should look at labour costs as a whole, not just net wage increases over the years.
After taxes and deductions for social security, Belgian net wages are between 45 and 60 percent of gross wages.
The culprit is the government, the unions say.

Aware of its key role in mediating between unions and employers, whose hardline positions have kept the two sides from doing a deal themselves, the government recently again imposed wage curbs for two years, extending a previous two-year ceiling.
The measure underscores Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's firm desire to act on job creation in the runup to the final stage of Europe's economic and monetary union due to be formed in 1999.
Making sure Belgium is among the frontrunners joining the EMU, or single currency, project is his other pet policy goal.
To create jobs Dehaene has tied the level of wage increases to those of Belgium's immediate neighbours, Germany, the Netherlands and France, who are also its main competitors.
Statistics show the tactic has worked.

Between 1987 and 1996 Belgian labour costs rose by 4.2 percent, outpacing its neighbours where costs were up only 3.8 percent. The rise was most noticeable in the first years of the period, before the introduction of the wage caps.
Once the measures were in place nominal wages increased by about one percentage point less in Belgium, figures show.

"The upper limit to wage increases laid down...should ensure a wage development which will remain conducive to employment during the years to come," a recent newsletter from the main dealers in Belgian government debt said.
Interested in taking over the Vilvoorde Renault plant, a Korean car maker on Thursday pointed out that labour costs in Belgium "were much lower than in Germany."
In the Renault case, singling out Belgian cost levels as a reason for the closure appears to have been a miscalculation by the French company, in which the French state has 46 percent.
More likely, protecting French jobs -- part of Vilvoorde's output is to go to plants in France -- was a driving factor behind the decision, Belgian unions say.
